opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I go back and forth on a lot, because there's a real tension. As researchers we're always tempted to build the general thing. You solve a problem once and think, "I could abstract this, other people would want this," and before you know it you've spent six months building infrastructure instead of doing the science you set out to do.

My rough heuristic is that a library is worth building when you notice you've solved essentially the same problem three or four times, in slightly different guises, and each time you're reinventing the same machinery. That repetition tells you the abstraction is real rather than one you've imagined in advance. If you build it too early, you bake in assumptions from the first use case, and they turn out to be wrong for the second and third.

The other thing I think about is whether the library changes what people can *express*, not just how fast they can do it. In probabilistic programming, for example, the value was never only convenience. Once you have the right primitives for conditioning and inference, you can think thoughts about models that were awkward or impossible before. When a library gives you a new vocabulary like that, it can be transformative. When it's just a wrapper around stuff people could already do easily, it's often not worth the maintenance burden.

And maintenance is the part people underestimate. A library is a commitment. Someone has to keep it working, document it, answer issues, keep up with dependencies. In an academic or small-lab setting, that's hard to sustain because the incentives reward papers, not software. So I also ask: is there a community, or at least a few people, who will actually use this and maybe help carry it? If it's just me, a well-organized research codebase is often the more honest choice.

So I'd summarize it as: wait until the pattern is clear, build it if it gives people new expressive power, and be realistic about who's going to look after it afterward.

r001.rationale: The response ties a library’s value to repeated uses, usefulness to other people, and whether the abstraction holds across later use cases.

r002.rationale: It does not compare building reusable structures in the mind to caching computations for anticipated future use.

r003.rationale: It offers heuristics for deciding when to build a library but does not propose rational decision theory as a framework.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot, partly because I've been burned by it in both directions. I've spent months building what I thought was a general-purpose library and then realized I was the only user, and I've also hacked together scripts that I ended up copy-pasting into five different projects, which is its own kind of pain.

The way I've come to think about it is that a library is really a bet. It's a bet that there's some abstraction that's stable across a bunch of use cases that you haven't fully seen yet. And the problem is that when you're building it, you usually only have one or two concrete use cases in front of you. So the question is, how confident are you that the thing you're pulling out is actually the invariant, and not just an artifact of the particular problem you happen to be working on?

In my experience, the honest answer is that you often can't know up front. So the heuristic I use is something like, don't build the library first. Solve the concrete problem, maybe solve it two or three times in slightly different contexts, and then look at what survived. The stuff that's identical across all of them, that's your library. The stuff that changed every time, that's not an abstraction, that's just you not knowing what you're doing yet, and freezing it in a library prematurely is actively harmful because now you have an interface you have to maintain and work around.

There's a second thing, which is more about the nature of the thing you're building. Some ideas are inherently compositional. Probabilistic programming is a good example. The whole point is that you want inference algorithms and models to be decoupled, so that you can mix and match. In that setting, building the library isn't a side project, it's actually the research. The abstraction is the contribution. If you can't articulate the interface cleanly, you probably don't understand the idea yet. So there I'd say the library-building is worthwhile almost by definition, because it's a forcing function for clarity.

And then the opposite case is where the thing you're building is very much tied to a specific model, a specific dataset, a specific experiment. There, I think people overinvest in generality. You see this a lot in machine learning research code, where someone writes a config system with forty options and a plugin architecture for a paper that's going to run one set of experiments. The generality is a kind of procrastination. It feels productive, but you're building for imaginary future users instead of answering the question in front of you.

So I guess the short version is, build the library when the abstraction is the point, or when you've empirically seen it recur. Don't build it because you have a vague sense that someone might want it someday. And be willing to throw the library away. One of the biggest mistakes is treating the existence of the library as evidence that it was the right abstraction. Sometimes you just need to admit it was wrong and start over.

r001.rationale: It describes a library as a bet on an abstraction remaining useful across multiple use cases, including future ones.

r002.rationale: It does not compare the mind’s construction of reusable structures to caching computations for anticipated future use.

r003.rationale: It offers practical heuristics but does not propose rational decision theory as a formal framework.

astra-6.text:
I think the question is whether you understand what ought to be reused. When you're working on a single problem, it's very easy to build something that looks general but actually encodes a lot of assumptions specific to that problem. So I tend to want a few concrete examples first. Solve those, and then see what structure they share.

There's also a cost beyond writing the code. You're creating an interface that someone has to understand, and you're committing to maintaining it. So a library is worthwhile when that interface makes subsequent problems substantially easier to solve. If using the abstraction requires more explanation than just solving the problem directly, that's a reason to wait.

r001.rationale: It weighs the library’s costs against whether its interface makes subsequent problems substantially easier, after examining concrete current examples.

r002.rationale: It does not liken the mind’s construction of reusable structures to caching computations for anticipated future use.

r003.rationale: It does not propose rational decision theory as a framework for deciding whether to build a library.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the question is whether you understand the thing well enough to know what ought to be reusable. When you’re exploring a problem, you’re often still discovering the right abstractions. If you turn those into a library too early, you can end up committing to assumptions that make the next problem harder to solve.

So I’d usually start with concrete applications and let some repetition happen. Then you can ask: what’s actually common across these cases, and what only looks similar? A library becomes worthwhile when there’s a stable core that lets you solve new problems with less effort, without having to fight the interface. And you have to count the work of documentation and maintenance, too—not just the code you avoid writing twice.

r001.rationale: It says a library is worthwhile when a stable core helps solve new problems with less effort, while accounting for documentation and maintenance costs.

r002.rationale: It discusses discovering reusable abstractions and avoiding premature commitment, but does not liken mental construction to caching computations for future use.

r003.rationale: It gives practical considerations but does not propose rational decision theory as a formal framework.
